theory.intro: A chord's length is tied to the angle it makes at the centre and to its distance from the centre. Each **chord property** below comes from congruent triangles built on two radii.
facts: Because $OA = OB$ are radii, the line from $O$ that bisects chord $AB$ also bisects $\angle AOB$.
steps: Identify which chord property matches the given information — equal chords, a right angle at the centre, or two intersecting circles.
Mark the equal lengths, equal angles or right angle the property gives.
Write an equation from the property, using Pythagoras' theorem where a right-angled triangle is formed.

foundation.solution_text:
$AB = CD$ (given)
$\angle COD = \angle AOB$ (equal chords subtend equal angles at the centre)
$x = 70^{\circ}$

$\angle AOB = \angle COD$ (given)
$AB = CD$ (equal angles at the centre give equal chords)
$x = 3.5$ m

$AB = CD$ (given)
$OE = OF$ (equal chords are equidistant from the centre)
$x = 7.2$ cm

$OE = OF$ (given)
$CD = AB$ (chords equidistant from the centre are equal)
$x = 9$ m

The perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord.
$AM = 10 \div 2$
$= 5$ cm

The perpendicular bisector of a chord passes through the centre, so $OM \perp AB$.
$x = \angle OMB = 90^{\circ}$

$OA = OB$ (radii) and $\angle AOM = \angle BOM$ (given), with $OM$ common, so $\triangle OAM \equiv \triangle OBM$ (SAS).
$\angle OMA = \angle OMB$ (matching angles of congruent triangles)
$\angle OMA + \angle OMB = 180^{\circ}$ (angles on a straight line $AB$)
$x = \angle OMB = 90^{\circ}$

development.solution_text:
$OZ \perp XY$, so $Z$ is the midpoint of $XY$ (perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord)
$XZ = 8 \div 2 = 4$ cm
$OX = OY$ (radii) and $OZ$ is common, so $\triangle OXZ \equiv \triangle OYZ$, so $OZ$ also bisects $\angle XOY$
$\angle XOZ = 102^{\circ} \div 2 = 51^{\circ}$

$AB = 16$ cm, so $AM = 8$ cm (perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord)
In right-angled $\triangle OAM$: $OA = 10$ cm, $AM = 8$ cm
$OM = \sqrt{OA^2 - AM^2}$
$= \sqrt{10^2 - 8^2}$
$= \sqrt{100 - 64}$
$= \sqrt{36}$
$= 6$ cm

In right-angled $\triangle OAM$: $OA = 13$ cm, $OM = 5$ cm
$AM = \sqrt{OA^2 - OM^2}$
$= \sqrt{13^2 - 5^2}$
$= \sqrt{169 - 25}$
$= \sqrt{144}$
$= 12$ cm
$AB = 2 \times AM$ (perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord)
$= 24$ cm

In right-angled $\triangle OAM$: $OA = 9$ cm, $OM = 4$ cm
$AM = \sqrt{OA^2 - OM^2}$
$= \sqrt{9^2 - 4^2}$
$= \sqrt{81 - 16}$
$= \sqrt{65}$ cm
$AB = 2 \times AM$ (perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord)
$= 2\sqrt{65}$ cm

$PQ$ joins the centres of the two intersecting circles, so it bisects the common chord $AB$ at right angles at $M$.
In right-angled $\triangle PAM$: $PA = 10$ cm, $PM = 6$ cm
$AM = \sqrt{PA^2 - PM^2}$
$= \sqrt{10^2 - 6^2}$
$= \sqrt{100 - 36}$
$= \sqrt{64}$
$= 8$ cm
$AB = 2 \times AM$ ($M$ is the midpoint of $AB$)
$= 16$ cm

$AM$ is half of $AB$, and $CN$ is half of $CD$ (perpendicular from the centre bisects each chord)
$AB = CD$ (given), so their halves are equal
$CN = AM = 6$ cm

For $AB$: half-chord $= 8$ cm, distance from centre $= \sqrt{10^2 - 8^2} = \sqrt{36} = 6$ cm
For $CD$: half-chord $= 6$ cm, distance from centre $= \sqrt{10^2 - 6^2} = \sqrt{64} = 8$ cm
$6$ cm $< 8$ cm, so $AB$, the longer chord, is closer to the centre.

mastery.solution_text:
In $\triangle OAM$ and $\triangle OBM$:
$\angle OMA = \angle OMB = 90^{\circ}$ (given, $OM \perp AB$)
$OA = OB$ (equal radii)
$OM = OM$ (common)
$\therefore \triangle OAM \equiv \triangle OBM$ (RHS)
$AM = BM$ (matching sides of congruent triangles)
$\therefore$ the perpendicular from the centre of a circle bisects the chord.

$OA = OB$ (radii), so $\triangle OAB$ is isosceles, giving $\angle OBA = \angle OAB$.
$OA = OC$ (radii), so $\triangle OAC$ is isosceles, giving $\angle OCA = \angle OAC$.
$\angle OAB = \angle OAC$ (given), so $\angle OBA = \angle OCA$.
In $\triangle OAB$ and $\triangle OAC$:
$\angle OAB = \angle OAC$ (given)
$\angle OBA = \angle OCA$ (shown above)
$OA = OA$ (common)
$\therefore \triangle OAB \equiv \triangle OAC$ (AAS)
$AB = AC$ (matching sides of congruent triangles)

a. In $\triangle ACD$ and $\triangle BCD$:
$AD = BD$ (equal radii of circle $D$)
$AC = BC$ (equal radii of circle $C$)
$CD = CD$ (common)
$\therefore \triangle ACD \equiv \triangle BCD$ (SSS)
b. $\angle ACD = \angle BCD$ (matching angles of congruent triangles), i.e. $\angle ACE = \angle BCE$
In $\triangle ACE$ and $\triangle BCE$:
$AC = BC$ (equal radii of circle $C$)
$\angle ACE = \angle BCE$ (shown above)
$CE = CE$ (common)
$\therefore \triangle ACE \equiv \triangle BCE$ (SAS)
c. $\angle AEC = \angle BEC$ (matching angles of congruent triangles)
$\angle AEC + \angle BEC = 180^{\circ}$ (angles on a straight line $AB$)
$\therefore \angle AEC = \angle BEC = 90^{\circ}$, so $CD \perp AB$
$AE = BE$ (matching sides of congruent triangles), so $E$ is the midpoint of $AB$
